01.title: Installing Git & Init Basics
01.theory: Learn how to install Git, configure user identity, and initialize repositories. Understand the hidden .git folder and file states.
examples: Initialize a repo and check status
notes: Config can be local, global, or system
Deleting .git removes history but not files

02.title: Making Commits
02.theory: Commits are snapshots of your project history. They record staged changes with a message and form the backbone of Git history.

03.title: Branching
03.theory: Branches allow parallel development. Each branch is a pointer to a commit, enabling experimentation without affecting main.
examples: Create and switch to a new branch
notes: Use branches for features or fixes

04.title: HEAD & References
04.theory: HEAD is a pointer to your current branch or commit. Learn how Git uses references to track branches and commits.
notes: HEAD usually points to the latest commit on the current branch

05.title: Reset & Revert
05.theory: Reset moves HEAD to a different commit, optionally changing the index and working directory. Revert creates a new commit that undoes changes.
notes: Revert is safer for shared repos

06.title: Rebase
06.theory: Rebase rewrites commit history to create a linear timeline. Useful for keeping feature branches up to date.
notes: Use carefully to avoid rewriting shared history

07.title: Merging
07.theory: Merge integrates changes from one branch into another. Understand fast-forward vs. recursive merges and conflict resolution.

08.title: Reset (Advanced)
08.theory: Learn advanced reset options: soft, mixed, and hard. Understand how they affect the staging area and working directory.
examples: Undo commits but keep changes staged

09.title: Cherry-pick
09.theory: Cherry-pick applies a specific commit from one branch onto another. Useful for hotfixes.
examples: Apply a bug fix commit onto main

10.title: Working with Remotes
10.theory: Remotes connect your local repo to servers like GitHub. Learn push, pull, and fetch operations.

11.title: Visualization & Debugging
11.theory: Use tools like git log, gitk, and visualization commands to understand history. Learn bisect for debugging.

12.title: GitHub Workflow
12.theory: A typical GitHub workflow involves branching, committing, pushing, and creating pull requests. Learn collaboration patterns.
examples: Create a feature branch and push it to GitHub
notes: Always open a pull request for review
